questions.title: Connection refused by the host script
questions.prompt:
The host Python script encounters the following error when connecting to `localhost:12434`. `docker model run ai/smollm2` works on the same PC.

```text
httpx.ConnectError: [Errno 61] Connection refused
  while connecting to localhost:12434
```

Which action resolves the issue?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Docker Desktop (macOS), Docker Model Runner

**Scenario:** A team is building a local development environment for an internal chatbot on MacBooks running Docker Desktop. They enabled Docker Model Runner on the AI settings tab and downloaded the model with `docker model pull ai/smollm2`. `docker model run ai/smollm2` responds normally in the terminal. However, a Python script on the host, an API server in a Compose container, and a browser frontend each fail to call the model. Each question concerns a different caller.

| Caller | Execution location | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python script | Host process | Uses the OpenAI SDK and attempts to connect on documented port 12434 |
| API server | Compose container | Receives the model runner address through an environment variable |
| Frontend | Browser (served from `http://localhost:3131`) | Calls the model runner API directly |

options.text: Reinstall the runner by running `docker model install-runner` again.
Change the script’s server address to `http://model-runner.docker.internal`.
Enable “Enable host-side TCP support” on Docker Desktop’s AI settings tab and specify the port.
Pull the model again with the `ai/smollm2:360M-Q4_K_M` tag.
Set the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable and rerun the script.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** The working `docker model run` command shows that the runner is installed and running. The issue is TCP access from the host process.

- **{{option:B}}.** This is the container access address. Host processes use `localhost` and the TCP port.

- **{{option:C}}.** Host-side TCP support must be enabled for host processes to access `http://localhost:12434`. Otherwise the port is not open and the connection is refused.

- **{{option:D}}.** The CLI already receives model responses. A refusal at the connection stage is not a model image or tag issue.

- **{{option:E}}.** DMR ignores the `Authorization` header and does not require an API key. Connection refusal occurs at the TCP stage, before authentication.

**Source documentation** https://github.com/docker/docs/blob/7efe900/content/manuals/ai/model-runner/get-started.md · https://github.com/docker/docs/blob/7efe900/content/manuals/ai/model-runner/api-reference.md · As of 2026-10-20 · docker/docs commit 7efe900 · Verification: documentation compared

questions.title: Environment variables injected by short syntax
questions.prompt: In an environment supporting this draft, which model-related environment variables are injected into `app` when running `docker compose up`?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Docker Compose, Docker Model Runner

**Scenario:** An AI service team wants to replace manually configured container model addresses with model declarations in the top-level `models` element of compose.yaml, injecting addresses and names automatically. Backend service `app` uses chat and embedding models. Some code already reads fixed environment variable names such as `AI_MODEL_URL`. The draft and CI runner details follow. Each question concerns a different issue.

```yaml
# Draft compose.yaml
services:
  app:
    image: registry.example.com/chat-app:1.4
    models:
      - chat-llm
      - embedding-model
models:
  chat-llm:
    model: ai/smollm2
  embedding-model:
    model: ai/all-minilm
```

```text
# CI runner
$ docker compose version
Docker Compose version v2.35.1
```

options.text: Two variables: `MODELS_CHAT_LLM`, `MODELS_EMBEDDING_MODEL`
`CHAT-LLM_URL`, `CHAT-LLM_MODEL`, `EMBEDDING-MODEL_URL`, `EMBEDDING-MODEL_MODEL`
`CHAT_LLM_URL`, `CHAT_LLM_MODEL`, `EMBEDDING_URL`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL`
`CHAT_LLM_URL`, `CHAT_LLM_MODEL`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL_URL`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL_MODEL`
`CHAT_LLM_ENDPOINT`, `CHAT_LLM_NAME`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL_ENDPOINT`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL_NAME`

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Short syntax creates two variables per model: an endpoint (`_URL`) and model identifier (`_MODEL`), not one.

- **{{option:B}}.** Hyphens are replaced with underscores and names uppercased. The documented example turns `embedding-model` into `EMBEDDING_MODEL_URL`.

- **{{option:C}}.** The prefix uses the entire model name, `EMBEDDING_MODEL`. A shortened name such as `EMBEDDING_URL` requires an explicit `endpoint_var`.

- **{{option:D}}.** Short syntax uppercases the model name, replaces hyphens with underscores, and appends `_URL` and `_MODEL`. Thus `embedding-model` produces `EMBEDDING_MODEL_URL` and `EMBEDDING_MODEL_MODEL`.

- **{{option:E}}.** The default suffixes are `_URL` and `_MODEL`, not `_ENDPOINT` and `_NAME`. Custom names require long syntax.

**Source documentation** https://github.com/docker/docs/blob/7efe900/content/manuals/compose/how-tos/models-and-compose.md · As of 2026-10-20 · docker/docs commit 7efe900 · Verification: documentation compared

```yaml
        model_var: AI_EMB_URL
```

- **{{option:C}}.** A short-syntax model named `ai_model` produces `AI_MODEL_URL`, but its identifier variable is `AI_MODEL_MODEL`, not the required `AI_MODEL_NAME`.

- **{{option:D}}.** Writing addresses and model names directly in `environment` violates the no-hardcoding requirement. Model definitions are also missing.

- **{{option:E}}.** `endpoint_var` carries the address and `model_var` the model identifier. Reversing them supplies the wrong values to the application.

questions.title: Configuration validation is rejected
questions.prompt:
The `llm-a` definition fails validation as follows.

```yaml
services:
  llm-a:
    image: nvidia/cuda:12.9.0-base-ubuntu22.04
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 1
```

```text
validating compose.yaml: services.llm-a.deploy.resources.reservations.devices.0
missing property 'capabilities'
```

How should it be fixed?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Docker Compose (server with four NVIDIA GPUs)

**Scenario:** The inference host has NVIDIA drivers and four GPUs, indexed 0 through 3. Team members configured per-service GPU reservations under `deploy.resources.reservations.devices` in compose.yaml. Some configurations are rejected; others receive an unintended number of GPUs. Each question covers one service and provides its definition.

| Service | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| llm-a | One GPU |
| llm-b | Only GPUs 0 and 3 |
| llm-c | All four host GPUs |
| embedder | One GPU |

options.text: Replace `count: 1` with `device_ids: ['0']`.
Add `capabilities: [gpu]` to the same `devices` entry.
Remove `driver: nvidia`.
Add `gpu: true` under `options`.
Replace `reservations` with `limits` to define GPU devices.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** `device_ids` specifies which GPUs to use and cannot replace `capabilities`; the missing-field error remains.

- **{{option:B}}.** `capabilities` is the only mandatory field in a `devices` entry and takes a string list such as `[gpu]`. Deployment fails if it is absent.

- **{{option:C}}.** `driver` is optional. Removing it does not supply required `capabilities`.

- **{{option:D}}.** `options` passes driver-specific key-value settings, not a substitute for `capabilities`.

- **{{option:E}}.** The documented GPU reservation location is `deploy.resources.reservations.devices`. Moving it does not supply the missing field.

**Source documentation** https://github.com/docker/docs/blob/7efe900/content/manuals/compose/how-tos/gpu-support.md · https://github.com/docker/docs/blob/7efe900/content/reference/compose-file/deploy.md · As of 2026-10-20 · docker/docs commit 7efe900 · Docker Compose v5.5.1 (error reproduced with `docker compose config`) · Verification: execution checked

Remove `device_ids`, leaving only `count: 2`.

questions.prompt:

```yaml

    deploy:
      resources:

          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 8
```

**Scenario:** The inference host has NVIDIA drivers and four GPUs, indexed 0 through 3. Team members configured per-service GPU reservations under `deploy.resources.reservations.devices` in compose.yaml. Some configurations are rejected; others receive an unintended number of GPUs. Change `capabilities` to `all` to request all capabilities.
The count exceeds the host’s four GPUs; reduce `count` to 4.
Set `replicas: 2` to split the GPU request across two containers.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** `count` and `device_ids` cannot coexist; this introduces another error.

- **{{option:B}}.** `capabilities` lists device capabilities such as `gpu`, not GPU quantity.

- **{{option:C}}.** The documentation states that requesting a `count` greater than the host’s GPU count causes an error. Set `count: 4` for the four required GPUs.

questions.prompt: After the last request at 02:00, both metrics begin reporting inactive (zero). There is one replica at that time. With this configuration, when is `rag-api` most likely to reach zero replicas?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Kubernetes, KEDA

**Scenario:** The internal RAG API `rag-api` slows down under morning traffic. The draft explicitly sets the default pollingInterval and cooldownPeriod, but omits metricType.

```yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: {name: rag-api}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {name: rag-api}
  pollingInterval: 30
  cooldownPeriod: 300

  maxReplicaCount: 20
```

Immediately at 02:00

- **{{option:D}}.** With one replica, HPA’s one-to-N behavior, including its scale-down stabilization window, does not intervene. KEDA handles zero-to-one transitions using cooldownPeriod.

- **{{option:E}}.** KEDA, not HPA, handles zero-to-one transitions. `minReplicaCount: 0` permits scaling to zero.

questions.prompt: A multi-turn chatbot records each user request as a separate trace. How can the Python SDK group these traces into one user session in Datadog?

options.text: Use a different ml_app for each user.
Add session_id to every span’s metrics.
Pass the session ID string as session_id when starting each request’s root span.
Use @workflow with the user ID as name for every request.
Change DD_LLMOBS_SESSION_ID per request.

- **{{option:B}}.** metrics holds numeric values, not session identifiers.

- **{{option:C}}.** The documentation says to pass the user-session string through session_id when starting the root span of a new trace; it is recorded as a span tag.

- **{{option:D}}.** name is the span name, not the session identity.

questions.title: OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute names
questions.prompt: Teams use different model providers. For vendor-neutral instrumentation, which OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-convention attributes record the provider and input token count on an LLM span?

options.text: `gen_ai.provider.name`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`
`gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`
`llm.vendor`, `llm.usage.tokens`
`gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`
`gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.response.id`

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** gen_ai.provider.name identifies the provider and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens counts input tokens. Both exist in the GenAI convention registry.

- **{{option:B}}.** gen_ai.system is the old name. Datadog marks it deprecated and recommends gen_ai.provider.name.

- **{{option:C}}.** These names are not in the convention.

- **{{option:D}}.** gen_ai.operation.name specifies an operation such as chat or embeddings; gen_ai.usage.output_tokens counts output tokens.

- **{{option:E}}.** gen_ai.request.model is the requested model and gen_ai.response.id the response identifier, not provider or input tokens.

questions.title: Sampling and cost metrics
questions.prompt: AI Observability billing grows with span delivery volume, so the Python SDK is configured with DD_LLMOBS_SAMPLE_RATE=0.1. Finance estimates LLM spending through ml_obs.span.llm.total.cost and token dashboards. How do these metrics change after sampling?

options.text: They fall to approximately one tenth and must be multiplied by ten.
They aggregate retained traces only, automatically extrapolating using the sample rate.
Only ml_obs.span.duration changes; cost/token metrics do not.
They do not change: metrics are calculated from all traffic independently of sampling.
Sampling disables automatic pricing, so cost metrics stop.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Sampling does not reduce metrics; no correction is needed.

- **{{option:B}}.** Metrics are not derived only from retained traces and do not use sampling-rate extrapolation.

- **{{option:C}}.** All ml_obs.* metrics are unaffected, including ml_obs.span.duration.

- **{{option:D}}.** Sampling discards spans after Datadog receives traces, so ml_obs.* metrics, including cost/tokens, reflect all traffic regardless of sample rate. Sampling reduces stored span volume and billing.

- **{{option:E}}.** Automatic cost calculation operates independently of sampling.

guide:
### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam assesses whether candidates can package and deploy existing AI services in containers and operate them reliably using observability and evaluation.

**Objectives**

- Configure AI service environments with Docker images and Compose.
- Interpret Kubernetes deployments, probes, resource settings, and autoscaling.
- Manage model registration, serving, search, and access on data and model platforms.
- Use traces and cost metrics to identify service health and operational problems.
- Manage release risk and cost with evaluation gates, model aliases, rollback, and budgets.

### 2. Target candidates

- Backend engineers, data engineers, DevOps engineers, platform engineers

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- One to two years of backend, data, or DevOps experience and ALF-level knowledge are recommended. No prior certification is required to take the exam.
- Scope covers packaging, deployment, observability, and releases for existing AI services. General Kubernetes cluster/node administration and managed AI operations services from AWS, Azure, and Google are excluded.
- Application and agent logic belongs to ADA/AEP; model tuning and evaluation methodology to MOS; security attacks and defenses to SES; and policy/regulatory interpretation to AGS.
- Questions test interpretation of supplied configurations, code, commands, and metrics rather than memorization of console menus, prices, or version numbers. Required dates and thresholds are provided.

**Exam structure**

- The full exam contains 65 questions in 130 minutes, with a scaled passing score of 720 out of 1,000. All 85 questions in the current bank have five options and one correct answer. Code completion is displayed as a separate question type.
- The full exam randomly samples individual questions from the entire bank. The demo contains 10 randomly selected questions. Each case question includes the shared scenario needed to answer it.
- Questions share a case scenario but can be answered independently; no answer is required to solve the next question.

### 3. Content domains

| Domain | Reference questions | Target weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Containerization and packaging | 12 | 18.46% |
| 2. Kubernetes deployment and serving | 13 | 20.00% |
| 3. Data and model platform operations | 15 | 23.08% |
| 4. Observability and evaluation operations | 13 | 20.00% |
| 5. Releases, reliability, and cost | 12 | 18.46% |

Target weights are shown to two decimal places based on the full exam question counts. Actual domain and question-category mixes vary because questions are sampled individually.

**Domain 1: Containerization and packaging**

- Knowledge: Dockerfile best practices, multistage builds, .dockerignore, image tags, build secrets, Compose models and GPU reservations, Docker Model Runner, and Docker Scout
- Skills: Read configurations and commands to diagnose model connectivity, GPU reservation, and secret exposure issues.

**Domain 2: Kubernetes deployment and serving**

- Knowledge: Deployment rolling updates and rollback, startup/readiness/liveness probes, requests and limits, HPA, KEDA ScaledObject, Jobs and CronJobs, Secrets, and GPU requests
- Skills: Distinguish service readiness from traffic routing and choose deployment and scaling settings for resource and load requirements.

**Domain 3: Data and model platform operations**

- Knowledge: MLflow tracking, Unity Catalog model registry and aliases, Model Serving, privileges, Snowflake AI functions, Cortex Search, and Model Registry versions and aliases
- Skills: Operate registered models and search services and diagnose version references, privileges, and refresh issues.

**Domain 4: Observability and evaluation operations**

- Knowledge: Datadog LLM Observability instrumentation, Agent and agentless setup, span types, ml_obs metrics, cost_tags, OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes, and evaluation results
- Skills: Diagnose missing traces and cost increases from metrics and configurations and configure team-level observability.

**Domain 5: Releases, reliability, and cost**

- Knowledge: Evaluation gates and scorers, model alias promotion and rollback, fallback, rate limits, Databricks budgets, and Snowflake budgets and per-user quotas
- Skills: Use evaluation results in release decisions and distinguish budget alerts from enforced usage restrictions.
